extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of comedy, humor theorists, playwrights and critics
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/theoretical analysis of the principles that make forms, faces, gestures, social practices and situations comic, with concrete examples (caricature, stage devices, fashion, bureaucracy, body vs soul). Useful for understanding and producing comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitatability of deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person could successfully imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ordinary person can mimic a deformity, that capacity for imitation is a source of laughter. (Implicit example: hunchback suggesting an attitude that can be copied.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity / permanent grimace
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression is one that will make us think of something rigid and coagulated; it is a unique and permanent grimace that 'promises nothing more than it gives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with expressive beauty (stable yet mobile) — comic faces are those whose moral life 'has crystallised' into a fixed cast of features. Examples: faces always engaged in weeping, laughing, whistling, or 'eternally blowing an imaginary trumpet.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism, inelasticity and habitual contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatism, inelasticity, habit that has been contracted and maintained are clearly the causes why a face (or movement) makes us laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanical, stereotyped qualities explain comic effect and are intensified when linked to a deep-seated cause (e.g., absentmindedness, the soul 'hypnotised' by materiality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature as revelation of latent tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the caricaturist consists in detecting an imperceptible tendency in a face or form and rendering it visible by magnifying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration must serve to manifest distortions present 'in embryo' rather than be an end in itself. Caricature can be lifelike if it respects the underlying tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration must respect the original ground plan/direction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the caricaturist alters size but 'respects its ground plan'—lengthening a nose in the direction it was already being lengthened—he makes the feature 'indulge in a grin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misaligned or gratuitous exaggeration may fail to produce true comic effect; exaggeration is comic when it reads as the natural completion of an existing tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with gracefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic should be contrasted with gracefulness rather than beauty: it partakes of rigidity and unsprightliness rather than of elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect often emerges where matter resists the soul's suppleness; if movement is petrified or immobilised, the result is comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanization of attitudes, gestures and movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear image of a person as a 'jointed puppet'—the more we see a set-up mechanism inside—heightens the comic. Study of comic artists shows this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for both clarity and subtlety in the machine-suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion must be a clear one (we must distinctly perceive a mechanism) and also a subtle one (the person must still appear living).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best comic drawing lets the two images—a living person and a machine—fit into each other so the artist imparts life to a puppet. Overly blunt mechanisation kills the living impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / identical movement implying automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain movement always the same, returning at regular intervals, when expected, causes involuntary laughter because it reveals a machine at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public speakers whose gestures repeat predictably invite laughter; life is expected to change, so repetition signals artificial mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes mechanical uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that never seemed laughable become so when imitated; imitation brings out the element of automatism in a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To imitate someone is to isolate the mechanical uniformity in their gesture, and that exposure is the essence of the ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflection of gestures toward mechanical occupations (parody device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures become more laughable when they are deflected—without altering form—towards some mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil, tugging imaginary ropes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody commonly uses this device: connecting a neutral gesture to a simple operation makes the mechanical reading explicit and increases comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and synchrony (marionette effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several people mirror one another—simultaneously striking the same attitudes—the uniformity makes them seem like marionettes and intensifies laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more numerous the identical images, the stronger the hallucination of invisible threads and the comic result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage contrivances as clockwork arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices like periodical repetition of a word/scene, systematic inversion of parts, or geometrical development of a farcical misunderstanding derive comic force from presenting an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events while preserving an outward aspect of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights achieve comic effect by making structural artifice visible enough to suggest mechanism, but plausible enough to retain life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise / fashion as source of comic via contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: A garment or fashion becomes ridiculous when its inert rigidity is contrasted with the living suppleness of the body; a break with continuity (anachronistic dress) exposes the garment as disguise and elicits laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar fashions hide their comic quality; only when continuity is broken (eccentric dressing) does the comic aspect emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent comic vs habituation; role of sudden dissolution of continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things are comic 'de jure' but not comic 'de facto' because continuity of custom deadens their comic quality; a sudden dissolution of continuity is needed to bring the comic to notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple explanations like 'surprise' or 'contrast' are incomplete — the key is uncovering a latent mechanical relation that habit obscures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic of imagination perceiving traits as disguise/artificial
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination operates by a logic (different from reason) that may perceive natural traits as artificially applied (e.g., a black face as 'daubed' or a red nose as painted), thereby transferring disguise's comic quality to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'imagination logic' is like societal dreams; recognizing when imagination reads a trait as artificial helps explain why some attributes provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial tampering with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where nature is 'mechanically tampered with' (half-clipped dog, artificially coloured flowers, plastered trees) are comic because they suggest masquerade or human artifice imposed on the natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To strengthen the comic, contrast the tampered image with the original natural source; literary and comic examples (Tartarin, Jerome K. Jerome) exploit this theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial / formulaic social actions as comic frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies and stereotyped social formulas are 'ready-made frames' that contain a latent comic element; isolating their form from their serious matter makes them laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any social ritual, from prize-distributions to court sittings, can become comic when attention is fixed on its form alone; the performers then resemble puppets following a formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative / bureaucratic automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials who perform duties like mere machines, or regulations that operate with inexorable fatality (applying rules absurdly), produce comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rescuees asked 'anything to declare' after shipwreck; MP claiming assassin 'got out the wrong side of the train, thereby infringing the Company's rules.' Bureaucratic pedantry amplifies the mechanical impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of human regulation/pedantry for natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: When human regulation or pedantry usurps the place of natural or moral law (regulating life as business routine), the mismatch is comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic imagination can turn pedantry into a caricature of nature, showing administration as a grotesque replacement of natural order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical intrusion where moral / intellectual is expected
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that calls attention to the physical (body) at a moment when the moral or intellectual side is expected (e.g., a sneeze during a pathetic speech) is comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bodily intrusions recall the body’s materiality and interrupt the expected soul-focused moment; Labiche and other comic writers exploit this contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting the body's materiality obstructing the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when the body appears as a heavy, cumbersome vesture or ballast that obstructs the soul's activity — the more petty and monotonous the body's claims, the more striking the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: characters distracted by toothache or tight shoes during moments that call for moral or eloquent expression; excessive stoutness evokes this image.
